entries.dbba48e6dabb1055f002ea210e14cba15d431c5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv32"/><title type="x-s3">Wisdom and Folly.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv32"/> <div sID="gen13814" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands. <div eID="gen13814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13815" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A good wife is a great blessing to a family. By a fruitful wife a family is multiplied and replenished with children, and so built up. But by a prudent wife, one that is pious, industrious, and considerate, the affairs of the family are made to prosper, debts are paid, portions raised, provision made, the children well educated and maintained, and the family has comfort within doors and credit without; thus is the house built. She looks upon it as her own to take care of, though she knows it is her husband's to bear rule in, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.22">Esth. i. 22</reference>. 2. Many a family is brought to ruin by ill housewifery, as well as by ill husbandry. A <hi type="italic">foolish</hi> woman, that has no fear of God nor regard to her business, that is wilful, and wasteful, and humoursome, that indulges her ease and appetite, and is all for jaunting and feasting, cards and the play-house, though she come to a plentiful estate, and to a family beforehand, she will impoverish and waste it, and will as certainly be the ruin of her house as if she <hi type="italic">plucked it down with her hands;</hi> and the husband himself, with all his care, can scarcely prevent it.
entries.3d370b105623dbc611d8af0e5dc7cc588ffa0c28: <div eID="gen13815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13816" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> He that walketh in his uprightness feareth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> perverse in his ways despiseth him. <div eID="gen13816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13817" type="x-p"/> Here are, 1. Grace and sin in their true colours. Grace reigning is a reverence of God, and gives honour to him who is infinitely great and high, and to whom all honour is due, than which what is more becoming or should be more pleasing to the rational creature? Sin reigning is no less than a contempt of God. In <hi type="italic">this,</hi> more than in any thing, sin appears exceedingly sinful, that it despises God, whom angels adore. Those that despise God's precepts, and will not be ruled by them, his promises, and will not accept of them, despise God himself and all his attributes. 2. Grace and sin in their true light. By this we may know a man that has grace, and the fear of God, reigning in him, <hi type="italic">he walks in his uprightness,</hi> he makes conscience of his actions, is faithful both to God and man, and every stop he makes, as well as every step he takes, is by rule; here is one that honours God. But, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">he that is perverse in his ways,</hi> that wilfully follows his own appetites and passions, that is unjust and dishonest and contradicts his profession in his conversation, however he may pretend to devotion, he is a wicked man, and will be reckoned with as a despiser of God himself.
entries.c122abd36c5dc10884a907b76635e1161481aa3b: <div eID="gen13817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> In the mouth of the foolish <hi type="italic">is</hi> a rod of pride: but the lips of the wise shall preserve them. <div eID="gen13818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13819" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. A proud fool exposing himself. Where there is pride in the heart, and no wisdom in the head to suppress it, it commonly shows itself in the words: <hi type="italic">In the mouth there is pride,</hi> proud boasting, proud censuring, proud scorning, proud commanding and giving law; this is the <hi type="italic">rod,</hi> or branch, <hi type="italic">of pride;</hi> the word is used only here and <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa. xi. 1</reference>. It grows from that root of bitterness which is in the heart; it is a rod from that stem. The root must be plucked up, or we cannot conquer this branch, or it is meant of a smiting beating rod, a <hi type="italic">rod of pride</hi> which strikes others. The proud man with his tongue lays about him and deals blows at pleasure, but it will in the end be a rod to himself; the proud man shall come under an ignominious correction by the words of his own mouth, not cut as a soldier, but caned as a servant; and herein he will be beaten with his own rod, <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. 2. A humble wise man saving himself and consulting his own good: <hi type="italic">The lips of the wise shall preserve them</hi> from doing that mischief to others which proud men do with their tongues, and from bringing that mischief on themselves which haughty scorners are often involved in.
entries.f6098d4d87560e218b4176d3da467c6afe228c27: <div eID="gen13819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13820" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Where no oxen <hi type="italic">are,</hi> the crib <hi type="italic">is</hi> clean: but much increase <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the strength of the ox. <div eID="gen13820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13821" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The neglect of husbandry is the way to poverty: <hi type="italic">Where no oxen are,</hi> to till the ground and tread out the corn, <hi type="italic">the crib</hi> is empty, <hi type="italic">is clean;</hi> there is no straw for the cattle, and consequently no bread for the service of man. Scarcity is represented by <hi type="italic">cleanness of teeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">Amos iv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Where no oxen are</hi> there is nothing to be done at the ground, and then nothing to be had out of it; <hi type="italic">the crib</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">is clean</hi> from dung, which pleases the neat and nice, that cannot endure husbandry because there is so much dirty work in it, and therefore will sell their oxen to keep the crib clean; but then not only the labour, but even the dung of the ox is wanted. This shows the folly of those who addict themselves to the pleasures of the country, but do not mind the business of it, who (as we say) keep more horses than kine, more dogs than swine; their families must needs suffer by it. 2. Those who take pains about their ground are likely to reap the profit of it. Those who keep that about them which is for use and service, not for state and show, more husbandmen than footmen, are likely to thrive. <hi type="italic">Much increase is by the strength of the ox;</hi> that is made for our service, and is profitable alive and dead.
entries.b384750ca4626888192fe73d75a4ba053f805911: <div eID="gen13821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13822" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> A faithful witness will not lie: but a false witness will utter lies. <div eID="gen13822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13823" type="x-p"/> In the administration of justice much depends upon the witnesses, and therefore it is necessary to the common good that witnesses be principled as they ought to be; for, 1. A witness that is conscientious will not dare to give in a testimony that is in the least untrue, nor, for good-will or ill-will, represent a thing otherwise than according to the best of his knowledge, whoever is pleased or displeased, and then judgment runs down like a river. 2. But a witness that will be bribed, and biassed, and browbeaten, <hi type="italic">will utter lies</hi> (and not stick nor startle at it), with as much readiness and assurance as if what he said were all true.
entries.b5fcdc72d45eff8fca51e5955129b3d3b709135b: <div eID="gen13823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13824" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> A scorner seeketh wisdom, and <hi type="italic">findeth it</hi> not: but knowledge <hi type="italic">is</hi> easy unto him that understandeth. <div eID="gen13824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13825" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The reason why some people seek wisdom, and do not find it, is because they do not seek it from a right principle and in a right manner. They are scorners, and it is in scorn that they ask instruction, that they may ridicule what is told them and may cavil at it. Many put questions to Christ, tempting him, and that they might have whereof to accuse him, but they were never the wiser. No marvel if those who seek wisdom, as Simon Magus sought the gifts of the Holy Ghost, to serve their pride and covetousness, do not find it, for they seek amiss. Herod desired to see a miracle, but he was a scorner, and therefore it was denied him, <reference osisRef="Luke.23.8">Luke xxiii. 8</reference>. Scorners speed not in prayer. 2. To those who understand aright, who <hi type="italic">depart from evil</hi> (for <hi type="italic">that is understanding</hi>), the <hi type="italic">knowledge</hi> of God and of his will <hi type="italic">is easy.</hi> The parables which harden scorners in their scorning, and make divine things more difficult to them, enlighten those who are willing to learn, and make the same things more plain, and intelligible, and familiar to them, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.11">Matt. xiii. 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.15">15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.16">16</reference>. The same word which to the scornful <hi type="italic">is a savour of death unto death</hi> to the humble and serious <hi type="italic">is a savour of life unto life.</hi> He <hi type="italic">that understands,</hi> so as to <hi type="italic">depart from evil</hi> (for <hi type="italic">that is understanding</hi>), to quit his prejudices, to lay aside all corrupt dispositions and affections, will easily apprehend instruction and receive the impressions of it.
entries.08da5a203f91cb726cbfbfdcd862d70302776f78: <div eID="gen13825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13826" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Go from the presence of a foolish man, when thou perceivest not <hi type="italic">in him</hi> the lips of knowledge. <div eID="gen13826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13827" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How we may discern a fool and discover him, a wicked man, for he is <hi type="italic">a foolish man.</hi> If we <hi type="italic">perceive not in him the lips of knowledge,</hi> if we find there is no relish or savour of piety in his discourse, that his communication is all corrupt and corrupting, and nothing in it <hi type="italic">good and to the use of edifying,</hi> we may conclude the treasure is bad. 2. How we must decline such a one and depart from him: <hi type="italic">Go from his presence,</hi> for <hi type="italic">thou perceivest</hi> there is no good to be gotten by his company, but danger of getting hurt by it. Sometimes the only way we have of reproving wicked discourse and witnessing against it is by leaving the company and going out of the hearing of it.
entries.700f690d355bc1eb332af5bc0684a955adcc1bfd: <div eID="gen13827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13828" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The wisdom of the prudent <hi type="italic">is</hi> to understand his way: but the folly of fools <hi type="italic">is</hi> deceit. <div eID="gen13828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13829" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. The good conduct of a wise and good man; he manages himself well. It is not the wisdom of the learned, which consists only in speculation, that is here recommended, but <hi type="italic">the wisdom of the prudent,</hi> which is practical, and is of use to direct our counsels and actions. Christian prudence consists in a right <hi type="italic">understanding of our way;</hi> for we are travellers, whose concern it is, not to spy wonders, but to get forward towards their journey's end. It <hi type="italic">is to understand our own way,</hi> not to be critics and busybodies in other men's matters, but to look well to ourselves and <hi type="italic">ponder the path of our feet,</hi> to understand the directions of our way, that we may observe them, the dangers of our way, that we may avoid them, the difficulties of our way, that we may break through them, and the advantages of our way, that we may improve them—to understand the rules we are to walk by and the ends we are to walk towards, and walk accordingly. 2. The bad conduct of a bad man; he puts a cheat upon himself. He does not rightly understand his way; he thinks he does, and so misses his way, and goes on in his mistake: <hi type="italic">The folly of fools is deceit;</hi> it cheats them into their own ruin. The folly of him that built on the sand was deceit.
entries.7cdc51b2e50090286241756a652e982f2174f93e: <div eID="gen13829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13830" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous <hi type="italic">there is</hi> favour. <div eID="gen13830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13831" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How wicked people are hardened in their wickedness: they <hi type="italic">make a mock at sin.</hi> They make a laughing matter of the sins of others, making themselves and their companions merry with that for which they should mourn, and they make a light matter of their own sins, both when they are tempted to sin and when they have committed it; they <hi type="italic">call evil good and good evil</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">Isa. v. 20</reference>), turn it off with a jest, rush into sin (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>) and say they shall have peace though they go on. They care not what mischief they do by their sins, and laugh at those that tell them of it. They are advocates for sin, and are ingenious at framing excuses for it. <hi type="italic">Fools make a mock at the sin-offering</hi> (so some); those that make light of sin make light of Christ. Those are fools that make light of sin, for they make light of that which God complains of (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.13">Amos ii. 13</reference>), which lay heavily upon Christ, and which they themselves will have other thoughts of shortly. 2. How good people are encouraged in their goodness: <hi type="italic">Among the righteous there is favour;</hi> if they in any thing offend, they presently repent and obtain the favour of God. They have a goodwill one to another; and among them, in their societies, there is mutual charity and compassion in cases of offences, and no mocking.
entries.791509e9e6b5c4a12f3b57ffb4a68d2e09e67801: <div eID="gen13831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13832" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy. <div eID="gen13832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13833" type="x-p"/> This agrees with <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.11">1 Cor. ii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">What man knows the things of a man,</hi> and the changes of his temper, <hi type="italic">save the spirit of a man?</hi> 1. Every man feels most from his own burden, especially that which is a burden upon the spirits, for that is commonly concealed and the sufferer keeps it to himself. We must not censure the griefs of others, for we know not what they feel; their stroke perhaps is heavier than their groaning. 2. Many enjoy a secret pleasure, especially in divine consolations, which others are not aware of, much less are sharers in; and, as the sorrows of a penitent, so the joys of a believer are such as a <hi type="italic">stranger does not intermeddle with</hi> and therefore is no competent judge of.
entries.4b2b3a70a1f2b234f01f95dba004290a5c14127e: <div eID="gen13833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish. <div eID="gen13834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13835" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sin is the ruin of great families: <hi type="italic">The house of the wicked,</hi> though built ever so strong and high, <hi type="italic">shall be overthrown,</hi> shall be brought to poverty and disgrace, and at length be extinct. His hope for heaven, the house on which he leans, shall not stand, but fail in the storm; the deluge that comes will sweep it away. 2. Righteousness is the rise and stability even of mean families: Even <hi type="italic">the tabernacle of the upright,</hi> though movable and despicable as a tent, <hi type="italic">shall flourish,</hi> in outward prosperity if Infinite Wisdom see good, at all events in graces and comfort, which are true riches and honours.
entries.7ca59dd5d83500696c75395e98dfe1cc5086aec3: <div eID="gen13835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13836" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof <hi type="italic">are</hi> the ways of death. <div eID="gen13836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13837" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the way and end of a great many self-deluded souls. 1. Their way is seemingly fair: It <hi type="italic">seems right</hi> to themselves; they please themselves with a fancy that they are as they should be, that their opinions and practices are good, and such as will bear them out. The way of ignorance and carelessness, the way of worldliness and earthly-mindedness, the way of sensuality and flesh-pleasing, seem right to those that walk in them, much more the way of hypocrisy in religion, external performances, partial reformations, and blind zeal; this they imagine will bring them to heaven; they flatter themselves in their own eyes that all will be well at last. 2. Their end is really fearful, and the more so for their mistake: It is <hi type="italic">the ways of death,</hi> eternal death; their iniquity will certainly be their ruin, and they will perish with a lie in their right hand. Self-deceivers will prove in the end self-destroyers.
entries.16c870733a11a8af08b28a7ec384d103d0002d13: <div eID="gen13837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13838" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth <hi type="italic">is</hi> heaviness. <div eID="gen13838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13839" type="x-p"/> This shows the vanity of carnal mirth, and proves what Solomon said of laughter, that <hi type="italic">it is mad;</hi> for, 1. There is sadness under it. Sometimes when sinners are under convictions, or some great trouble, they dissemble their grief by a forced mirth, and put a good face on it, because they will not seem to yield: they cry not when he binds them. Nay, when men really are merry, yet at the same time there is some alloy or other to their mirth, something that casts a damp upon it, which all their gaiety cannot keep from their heart. Their consciences tell them they have no reason to be merry (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.1">Hos. ix. 1</reference>); they cannot but see the vanity of it. Spiritual joy is seated in the soul; the joy of the hypocrite is but from the teeth outward. See <reference osisRef="John.16.22">John xvi. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2 Cor. vi. 10</reference>. 2. There is worse after it: <hi type="italic">The end of that mirth is heaviness.</hi> It is soon over, like the crackling of thorns under a pot; and, if the conscience be awake, all sinful and profane mirth will be reflected upon with bitterness; if not, the heaviness will be so much the greater when <hi type="italic">for all these things God shall bring the</hi> sinner <hi type="italic">into judgment.</hi> The sorrows of the saints will end in everlasting joys (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.5">Ps. cxxvi. 5</reference>), but the laughter of fools will end in endless weeping and wailing.  <div eID="gen13839" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d0a29b876bc0991fc4d7a8c5f1813ad9411523a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv33"/><title type="x-s3">The Righteous and the Wicked Contrasted.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv33"/> <div sID="gen13840" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways: and a good man <hi type="italic">shall be satisfied</hi> from himself. <div eID="gen13840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13841" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The misery of sinners will be an eternal surfeit upon their sins: The <hi type="italic">backslider in heart,</hi> who for fear of suffering, or in hope of profit or pleasure, forsakes God and his duty, shall be <hi type="italic">filled with his own ways;</hi> God will give him enough of them. They would not leave their brutish lusts and passions, and therefore they shall stick by them, to their everlasting terror and torment. <hi type="italic">He that is filthy shall be filthy still. "Son, remember,</hi>" shall <hi type="italic">fill them with their own ways,</hi> and set their sins in order before them. Backsliding begins in the heart; it is the evil heart of unbelief that departs from God; and of all sinners backsliders will have most terror when they reflect on <hi type="italic">their own ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.11.26">Luke xi. 26</reference>. 2. The happiness of the saints will be an eternal satisfaction in their graces, as tokens of and qualifications for God's peculiar favour: <hi type="italic">A good man shall be</hi> abundantly <hi type="italic">satisfied from himself,</hi> from what God has wrought in him. He has <hi type="italic">rejoicing in himself alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.3">Gal. vi. 3</reference>. As sinners never think they have sin enough till it brings them to hell, so saints never think they have grace enough till it brings them to heaven.
entries.263a9b1f43c2687a3b15ad25c979c9c5f8680b77: <div eID="gen13841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13842" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> The simple believeth every word: but the prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> looketh well to his going. <div eID="gen13842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13843" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is folly to be credulous, to heed every flying report, to give ear to every man's story, though ever so improbable, to take things upon trust from common fame, to depend upon every man's profession of friendship and give credit to every one that will promise payment; those are <hi type="italic">simple</hi> who thus <hi type="italic">believe every word,</hi> forgetting that all men, in some sense, are liars in comparison with God, all whose words we are to believe with an implicit faith, for he cannot lie. 2. It is wisdom to be cautious: <hi type="italic">The prudent man</hi> will try before he trusts, will weigh both the credibility of the witness and the probability of the testimony, and then give judgment as the thing appears or suspend his judgment till it appears. <hi type="italic">Prove all things,</hi> and <hi type="italic">believe not every spirit.</hi>
entries.407561562a01168a32df7cc78a51192e2ff44bc6: <div eID="gen13843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13844" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> A wise <hi type="italic">man</hi> feareth, and departeth from evil: but the fool rageth, and is confident. <div eID="gen13844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13845" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Holy fear is an excellent guard upon every holy thing, and against every thing that is unholy. It is wisdom to depart <hi type="italic">from evil,</hi> from the evil of sin, and thereby from all other evil; and therefore it is wisdom to fear, that is, to be jealous over ourselves with a godly jealousy, to keep up a dread of God's wrath, to be afraid of coming near the borders of sin or dallying with the beginnings of it. A wise man, for fear of harm, keeps out of harm's way, and starts back in a fright when he finds himself entering into temptation. 2. Presumption is folly. He who, when he is warned of his danger, <hi type="italic">rages and is confident,</hi> furiously pushes on, cannot bear to be checked, bids defiance to the wrath and curse of God, and, fearless of danger, persists in his rebellion, makes bold with the occasions of sin, and plays upon the precipice, he is a fool, for he acts against his reason and his interest, and his ruin will quickly be the proof of his folly.
entries.d00497d4b4c81642b055aad35bdaff8205ee97e1: <div eID="gen13845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> soon angry dealeth foolishly: and a man of wicked devices is hated. <div eID="gen13846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13847" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Passionate men are justly laughed at. Men who are peevish and touchy, and are <hi type="italic">soon angry</hi> upon every the least provocation, <hi type="italic">deal foolishly;</hi> they say and do that which is ridiculous, and so expose themselves to contempt; they themselves cannot but be ashamed of it when the heat is over. The consideration of this should engage those especially who are in reputation for wisdom and honour with the utmost care to bridle their passion. 2. Malicious men are justly dreaded and detested, for they are much more dangerous and mischievous to all societies: <hi type="italic">A man of wicked devices,</hi> who stifles his resentments till he has an opportunity of being revenged, and is secretly plotting how to wrong his neighbour and to do him an ill turn, as Cain to kill Abel, such a man as this is hated by all mankind. The character of an angry man is pitiable; through the surprise of a temptation he disturbs and disgraces himself, but it is soon over, and he is sorry for it. But that of a spiteful revengeful man is odious; there is no fence against him nor cure for him.
entries.932ed4ccabaef56a3dd7df71529c6f948a317020: <div eID="gen13847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> The simple inherit folly: but the prudent are crowned with knowledge. <div eID="gen13848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13849" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Sin is the shame of sinners: <hi type="italic">The simple,</hi> who love simplicity, get nothing by it; they <hi type="italic">inherit folly.</hi> They have it <hi type="italic">by inheritance,</hi> so some. This corruption of nature is derived from our first parents, and all the calamities that attend it we have by kind; it was the inheritance they transmitted to their degenerate race, an hereditary disease. They are as fond of it as a man of his inheritance, hold it as fast, and are as loth to part with it. What they value themselves upon is really foolish; and what will be the issue of their simplicity but folly? They will for ever rue their own foolish choice. 2. Wisdom is the honour of the wise: <hi type="italic">The prudent crown</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">with knowledge,</hi> they look upon it as their brightest ornament, and there is nothing they are so ambitious of; they bind it to their heads as a crown, which they will by no means part with; they press towards the top and perfection of knowledge, which will crown their beginnings and progress. They shall have the praise of it; wise heads shall be respected as if they were crowned heads. They <hi type="italic">crown knowledge</hi> (so some read it); they are a credit to their profession. Wisdom is not only justified, but glorified, of all her children.
entries.64f5aaf1af1ab5a57ff2c31d3c3b676c06fc467d: <div eID="gen13849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13850" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> The evil bow before the good; and the wicked at the gates of the righteous. <div eID="gen13850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13851" type="x-p"/> That is, 1. The wicked are oftentimes impoverished and brought low, so that they are forced to beg, their wickedness having reduced them to straits; while good men, by the blessing of God, are enriched, and enabled to give, and do give, even to the evil; for where God grants life we must not deny a livelihood. 2. Sometimes God extorts, even from bad men, an acknowledgement of the excellency of God's people. The evil ought always to <hi type="italic">bow before the good,</hi> and sometimes they are made to do it and <hi type="italic">to know that God has loved them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. They desire their favour (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.7">Esth. vii. 7</reference>), their prayers, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.12">2 Kings iii. 12</reference>. 3. There is a day coming when the upright shall have the dominion (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>), when the foolish virgins shall come begging to the wise for oil, and shall knock in vain at that gate of the Lord at which the righteous entered.
entries.5c08c73eb49b884f3dc91e86e1126bc42b8289fb: <div eID="gen13851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> The poor is hated even of his own neighbour: but the rich <hi type="italic">hath</hi> many friends. <div eID="gen13852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13853" type="x-p"/> This shows, not what should be, but what is the common way of the world—to be shy of the poor and fond of the rich. 1. Few will give countenance to those whom the world frowns upon, though otherwise worthy of respect: <hi type="italic">The poor,</hi> who should be pitied, and encouraged, and relieved, <hi type="italic">is hated,</hi> looked strange upon, and kept at a distance, even <hi type="italic">by his own neighbour,</hi> who, before he fell into disgrace, was intimate with him and pretended to have a kindness for him. Most are swallow-friends, that are gone in winter. It is good having God our friend, for he will not desert us when we are poor. 2. Every one will make court to those whom the world smiles upon, though otherwise unworthy: <hi type="italic">The rich have many friends,</hi> friends to their riches, in hope to get something out of them. There is little friendship in the world but what is governed by self-interest, which is no true friendship at all, nor what a wise man will either value himself on or put any confidence in. Those that make the world their God idolize those that have most of its good things, and seek their favour as if indeed they were Heaven's favourites.
entries.54488cc6644840ef2c33301384b502dd50336ed2: <div eID="gen13853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> he. <div eID="gen13854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13855" type="x-p"/> See here how men's character and condition are measured and judged of by their conduct towards their poor neighbours. 1. Those that look upon them with contempt have here assigned them a bad character, and their condition will be accordingly: <hi type="italic">He that despises his neighbour</hi> because he is low in the world, because he is of a mean extraction, rustic education, and makes but a mean figure, that thinks it below him to take notice of him, converse with him, or concern himself about him, and sets him with the dogs of his flock, <hi type="italic">is a sinner,</hi> is guilty of a sin, is in the way to worse, and shall be dealt with as a sinner; unhappy is he. 2. Those that look upon them with compassion are here said to be in a good condition, according to their character: <hi type="italic">He that has mercy on the poor,</hi> is ready to do all the good offices he can to him, and thereby puts an honour upon him, <hi type="italic">happy is he;</hi> he does that which is pleasing to God, which he himself will afterwards reflect upon with great satisfaction, for which the loins of the poor will bless him, and which will be abundantly recompensed in the resurrection of the just.
entries.a0bc9fae534e236edb6a5a1096aff14a1e43dea3: <div eID="gen13855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Do they not err that devise evil? but mercy and truth <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to them that devise good. <div eID="gen13856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13857" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How miserably mistaken those are that not only do evil, but devise it: <hi type="italic">Do they not err?</hi> Yes, certainly they do; every one knows it. They think that by sinning with craft and contrivance, and carrying on their intrigues with more plot and artifice than others, they shall make a better hand of their sins than others do, and come off better. But they are mistaken. God's justice cannot be out-witted. Those that devise evil against their neighbours greatly err, for it will certainly turn upon themselves and end in their own ruin, a fatal error! 2. How wisely those consult their own interest that not only do good but devise it: <hi type="italic">Mercy and truth</hi> shall be to them, not a reward of debt (they will own that they merit nothing), but a reward of mercy, mere mercy, mercy according to the promise, mercy and truth, to which God is pleased to make himself a debtor. Those that are so liberal as to devise liberal things, that seek opportunities of doing good, and contrive how to make their charity most extensive and most acceptable to those that need it, <hi type="italic">by liberal things they shall stand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 8</reference>.
entries.2e84d5f77cb511ebd5d6be7a8f529ac562ac2290: <div eID="gen13857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips <hi type="italic">tendeth</hi> only to penury. <div eID="gen13858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13859" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Working, without talking, will make men rich: <hi type="italic">In all labour</hi> of the head, or of the hand, <hi type="italic">there is profit;</hi> it will turn to some good account or other. Industrious people are generally thriving people, and where there is something done there is something to be had. <hi type="italic">The stirring hand gets a penny.</hi> It is good therefore to keep in business, and to keep in action, and what our hand finds to do to do it with all our might. 2. Talking, without working, will make men poor. Those that love to boast of their business and make a noise about it, and that waste their time in tittle-tattle, in telling and hearing new things, like the Athenians, and, under pretence of improving themselves by conversation, neglect the work of their place and day, they waste what they have, and the course they take <hi type="italic">tends to penury,</hi> and will end in it. It is true in the affairs of our souls; those that take pains in the service of God, that strive earnestly in prayer, will find profit in it. But if men's religion runs all out in talk and noise, and their praying is only the labour of the lips, they will be spiritually poor, and come to nothing.
entries.10bc4eff3b33b6a372aab872e7a78fa54c34fb20: <div eID="gen13859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13860" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The crown of the wise <hi type="italic">is</hi> their riches: <hi type="italic">but</hi> the foolishness of fools <hi type="italic">is</hi> folly. <div eID="gen13860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13861" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. If men be wise and good, riches make them so much the more honourable and useful: <hi type="italic">The crown of the wise is their riches;</hi> their riches make them to be so much the more respected, and give them the more authority and influence upon others. Those that have wealth, and wisdom to use it, will have a great opportunity of honouring God and doing good in the world. <hi type="italic">Wisdom is good</hi> without <hi type="italic">an inheritance,</hi> but better <hi type="italic">with</hi> it. 2. If men be wicked and corrupt, their wealth will but the more expose them: <hi type="italic">The foolishness of fools,</hi> put them in what condition you will, <hi type="italic">is folly,</hi> and will show itself and shame them; if they have riches, they do mischief with them and are the more hardened in their foolish practices.
entries.5bc1f91f52615c98fdfc13d06efc58ced608b74b: <div eID="gen13861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13862" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> A true witness delivereth souls: but a deceitful <hi type="italic">witness</hi> speaketh lies. <div eID="gen13862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13863" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How much praise is due to a faithful witness: He <hi type="italic">delivers the souls</hi> of the innocent, who are falsely accused, and their good names, which are as dear to them as their lives. A man of integrity will venture the displeasure of the greatest, to bring truth to light and rescue those who are injured by falsehood. A faithful minister, who truly witnesses for God against sin, is thereby instrumental to deliver souls from eternal death. 2. How little regard is to be had to a false witness. He forges <hi type="italic">lies,</hi> and yet pours them out with the greatest assurance imaginable for the destruction of the innocent. It is therefore the interest of a nation by all means possible to detect and punish false-witness-bearing, yea, and lying in common conversation; for truth is the cement of society.
entries.e92177317175b566f9e9856ef55528cb47cb385a: <div eID="gen13863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13864" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> In the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge. <hi type="super">27</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death. <div eID="gen13864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13865" type="x-p"/> In these two verses we are invited and encouraged to live in the fear of God by the advantages which attend a religious life. The <hi type="italic">fear of the Lord</hi> is here put for all gracious principles, producing gracious practices. 1. Where this reigns it produces a holy security and serenity of mind. There is in it a <hi type="italic">strong confidence;</hi> it enables a man still to hold fast both his purity and his peace, whatever happens, and gives him boldness before God and the world. <hi type="italic">I know that I shall be justified—None of these things move me;</hi> such is the language of this confidence. 2. It entails a blessing upon posterity. The children of those that by faith make God their confidence shall be encouraged by the promise that God will be a God to believers and to their seed to flee to him as their refuge, and they shall find shelter in him. The children of religious parents often do the better for their parents' instructions and example and fare the better for their faith and prayers. "<hi type="italic">Our fathers trusted in thee,</hi> therefore we will." 3. It is an over-flowing ever-flowing spring of comfort and joy; it is <hi type="italic">a fountain of life,</hi> yielding constant pleasure and satisfaction to the soul, joys that are pure and fresh, are life to the soul, and quench its thirst, and can never be drawn dry; it is a <hi type="italic">well of living water,</hi> that is springing up to, and is the earnest of, eternal life. 4. It is a sovereign antidote against sin and temptation. Those that have a true relish of the pleasures of serious godliness will not be allured by the baits of sin to swallow its hook; they know where to obtain better things than any it can pretend to offer, and therefore it is easy to them <hi type="italic">to depart from the snares of death</hi> and to keep their foot from being taken in them.
entries.fb9ad6a34e2ad2ab95c0c1ae223dda724ab3b7b5: <div eID="gen13865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13866" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> In the multitude of people <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king's honour: but in the want of people <hi type="italic">is</hi> the destruction of the prince. <div eID="gen13866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13867" type="x-p"/> Here are two maxims in politics, which carry their own evidence with them:—1. That it is much for the honour of a king to have a populous kingdom; it is a sign that he rules well, since strangers are hereby invited to come and settle under his protection and his own subjects live comfortably; it is a sign that he and his kingdom are under the blessing of God, the effect of which is being fruitful and multiplying. It is his strength, and makes him considerable and formidable; happy is the king, the father of his country, who has his <hi type="italic">quiver full of arrows;</hi> he <hi type="italic">shall not be ashamed, but shall speak with his enemy in the gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.4-Ps.127.5">Ps. cxxvii. 4, 5</reference>. It is therefore the wisdom of princes, by a mild and gentle government, by encouraging trade and husbandry, and by making all easy under them, to promote the increase of their people. And let all that wish well to the kingdom of Christ, and to his honour, do what they can in their places that many may be added to his church. 2. That when the people are lessened the prince is weakened: <hi type="italic">In the want of people is the leanness of the prince</hi> (so some read it); trade lies dead, the ground lies untilled, the army wants to be recruited, the navy to be manned, and all because there are not hands sufficient. See how much the honour and safety of kings depend upon their people, which is a reason why they should rule by love, and not with rigour. Princes are corrected by those judgments which abate the number of the people, as we find, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.13">2 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>.
entries.4a0ef64ee4d8cd62c247379235103e5120b96a8d: <div eID="gen13867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> slow to wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> of great understanding: but <hi type="italic">he that is</hi> hasty of spirit exalteth folly. <div eID="gen13868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13869" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Meekness is wisdom. <hi type="italic">He</hi> rightly understands himself, and his duty and interest, the infirmities of human nature, and the constitution of human society, who <hi type="italic">is slow to anger,</hi> and knows how to excuse the faults of others as well as his own, how to adjourn his resentments, and moderate them, so as by no provocation to be put out of the possession of his own soul. A mild patient man is really to be accounted an intelligent man, one that learns of Christ, who is Wisdom itself. 2. Unbridled passion is folly proclaimed: <hi type="italic">He that is hasty of spirit,</hi> whose heart is tinder to every spark of provocation, that is all fire and tow, as we say, he thinks hereby to magnify himself and make those about stand in awe of him, whereas really he <hi type="italic">exalts his own folly;</hi> he makes it known, as that which is lifted up is visible to all, and he submits himself to it as to the government of one that is exalted.
entries.02c0e475367b10d70c5da890ccd15940aa49515e: <div eID="gen13869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13870" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">30</hi> A sound heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones. <div eID="gen13870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13871" type="x-p"/> The foregoing verse showed how much our reputation, this how much our health, depends on the good government of our passions and the preserving of the temper of the mind. 1. A healing spirit, made up of love and meekness, a hearty, friendly, cheerful disposition, is <hi type="italic">the life of the flesh;</hi> it contributes to a good constitution of body; people grow fat with good humour. 2. A fretful, envious, discontented spirit, is its own punishment; it consumes the flesh, preys upon the animal spirits, makes the countenance pale, and is the <hi type="italic">rottenness of the bones.</hi> Those that see the prosperity of others and are grieved, let them <hi type="italic">gnash with their teeth and melt away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Ps. cxii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen13871" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen13872"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13873"/>Rumpatur, quisquis rumpitur invidia.<l eID="gen13873" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen13874"/>Whoever bursts for envy, let him burst.
entries.08a3de99778530c9cae7d56d00a3e1d9fe587ea4: <l eID="gen13874" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen13872"/> <div sID="gen13875" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor. <div eID="gen13875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13876" type="x-p"/> God is here pleased to interest himself more than one would imagine in the treatment given to the poor. 1. He reckons himself affronted in the injuries that are done them. Whosoever he be that wrongs a poor man, taking advantage against him because he is poor and cannot help himself, let him know that he puts an affront upon his Maker. God made him, and gave him his being, the same that is the author of our being; we have all one Father, one Maker; see how Job considered this, <reference osisRef="Job.31.15">Job xxxi. 15</reference>. God made him poor, and appointed him his lot, so that, if we deal hardly with any because they are poor, we reflect upon God as dealing hardly with them in laying them low, that they might be trampled upon. 2. He reckons himself honoured in the kindnesses that are done them; he takes them as done to himself, and will show himself accordingly pleased with them. <hi type="italic">I was hungry, and you gave me meat.</hi> Those therefore that have any true honour for God will show it by compassion to the poor, whom he has undertaken in a special manner to protect and patronise.
entries.f26f3a1657136fea09da5fda6d60e6c127129000: <div eID="gen13876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13877" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> The wicked is driven away in his wickedness: but the righteous hath hope in his death. <div eID="gen13877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13878" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The desperate condition of a wicked man when he goes out of the world: He <hi type="italic">is driven away in his wickedness.</hi> He cleaves so closely to the world that he cannot find in his heart to leave it, but is driven away out of it; his soul is required, is forced from him, And sin cleaves so closely to him that it is inseparable; it goes with him into another world; he <hi type="italic">is driven away in his wickedness,</hi> dies in his sins, under the guilt and power of them, unjustified, unsanctified. His wickedness is the storm in which he is hurried away, as chaff before the wind, chased out of the world. 2. The comfortable condition of a godly man when he finishes his course: He <hi type="italic">has hope in his death</hi> of a happiness on the other side death, of better things in another world than ever he had in this. <hi type="italic">The righteous</hi> then have the grace of hope in them; though they have pain, and some dread of death, yet they have hope. They have before them the good hoped for, even the blessed hope which God, who cannot lie, has promised.
entries.46f2a89e50270aee69983ae5c77d9fc82e9195ba: <div eID="gen13878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> Wisdom resteth in the heart of him that hath understanding: but <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> in the midst of fools is made known. <div eID="gen13879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13880" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Modesty is the badge of wisdom. He that is truly wise hides his treasure, so as not to boast of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Matt. xiii. 44</reference>), though he does not hide his talent, so as not to trade with it. His <hi type="italic">wisdom rests in his heart;</hi> he digests what he knows, and has it ready to him, but does not unseasonably talk of it and make a noise with it. The heart is the seat of the affections, and there wisdom must rest in the practical love of it, and not swim in the head. 2. Openness and ostentation are a mark of folly. If fools have a little smattering of knowledge, they take all occasions, though very foreign, to produce it, and bring it in by head and shoulders. Or the folly that <hi type="italic">is in the midst of fools is made known</hi> by their forwardness to talk. Many a foolish man takes more pains to show his folly than a wise man thinks it worth his while to take to show his wisdom.
entries.69e08a612c0ddaf8b744ae48b71e3530c286805a: <div eID="gen13880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13881" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin <hi type="italic">is</hi> a reproach to any people. <div eID="gen13881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13882" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Justice, reigning in a nation, puts an honour upon it. A righteous administration of the government, impartial equity between man and man, public countenance given to religion, the general practice and profession of virtue, the protecting and preserving of virtuous men, charity and compassion to strangers (<hi type="italic">alms</hi> are sometimes called <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi>), these <hi type="italic">exalt a nation;</hi> they uphold the throne, elevate the people's minds, and qualify a nation for the favour of God, which will make them high, as a <hi type="italic">holy nation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.26.19">Deut. xxvi. 19</reference>. 2. Vice, reigning in a nation, puts disgrace upon it: <hi type="italic">Sin is a reproach to any</hi> city or kingdom, and renders them despicable among their neighbours. The people of Israel were often instances of both parts of this observation; they were great when they were good, but when they forsook God all about them insulted them and trampled on them. It is therefore the interest and duty of princes to use their power for the suppression of vice and support of virtue.
entries.0da901ec5b6fa4c02f43955a2dd7569469b70969: <div eID="gen13882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13883" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">35</hi> The king's favour <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward a wise servant: but his wrath is <hi type="italic">against</hi> him that causeth shame. <div eID="gen13883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13884" type="x-p"/> This shows that in a well-ordered court and government smiles and favours are dispensed among those that are employed in public trusts according to their merits; Solomon lets them know he will go by that rule, 1. That those who behave themselves wisely shall be respected and preferred, whatever enemies they may have that seek to undermine them. No man's services shall be neglected to please a party or a favourite. 2. That those who are selfish and false, who betray their country, oppress the poor, and sow discord, and thus <hi type="italic">cause shame,</hi> shall be displaced and banished the court, whatever friends they may make to speak for them.  <chapter eID="Prov.14"/> <div eID="gen13884" type="x-p"/>

entries.13dfbde9587d72be74298674b7c6c2ac5965a74a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7484"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <div sID="gen11576" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Prov.14.1-Prov.14.35">Pr 14:1-35</reference>.<div eID="gen11576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7484"/><hi type="bold">1. Every wise, &c.--</hi>literally, "The wisdoms" (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Pr 9:1</reference>) "of women," plural, a distributive form of speech.<div eID="gen11577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buildeth ... house--</hi>increases wealth, which the foolish, by mismanagement, lessen. <div eID="gen11578" type="x-p"/>
entries.d058a49f0869c9d71d59e5ef9c377694d98ac89e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7485"/><div sID="gen11579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7485"/><hi type="bold">2. uprightness--</hi>is the fruit of fearing God, as falsehood and ill-nature (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pr 2:15</reference>; 3:32) of despising Him and His law. <div eID="gen11579" type="x-p"/>
entries.65e6b041ad61eb89224d1473b55e7e0445fecab2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7486"/><div sID="gen11580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7486"/><hi type="bold">3. rod of pride--</hi>that is, the punishment of pride, which they evince by their words. The words of the wise procure good to them. <div eID="gen11580" type="x-p"/>
entries.05c0a412a8c32c72a578846a5a762c9fbb1be694: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7487"/><div sID="gen11581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7487"/><hi type="bold">4. crib is clean--</hi>empty; so "cleanness of teeth" denotes want of food (compare <reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">Am 4:6</reference>). Men get the proper fruit of their doings (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>). <div eID="gen11581" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3a37e57ce12520f9ca394466a976649a8daf9f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7488"/><div sID="gen11582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7488"/><hi type="bold">5. A faithful witness, &c.--</hi>one tested to be such.<div eID="gen11582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">utter lies--</hi>or, "breathe out lies"--that is, habitually lies (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.19">Pr 6:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.9.1">Ac 9:1</reference>). Or the sense is, that habitual truthfulness, or lying, will be evinced in witness-bearing. <div eID="gen11583" type="x-p"/>

entries.8f6add60eb73db8c4edef024bfa4aea3bc672041: <div eID="gen24228" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24229" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24230" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24230" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24229" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24231" type="x-p"/> Various moral sentiments. The antithesis between wisdom and folly, and the different effects of each. <div eID="gen24231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24232" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24233" type="x-p"/> Every wise woman buildeth her house - By her prudent and industrious management she increases property in the family, furniture in the house, and food and raiment for her household. This is the true building of a house. The thriftless wife acts differently, and the opposite is the result. Household furniture, far from being increased, is dilapidated; and her household are ill-fed, ill-clothed, and worse educated.
entries.923d65e50df7f98873cad1fd431a686e368215e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24234" type="x-p"/> The mouth of the foolish is a rod of pride - The reproofs of such a person are ill-judged and ill-timed, and generally are conveyed in such language as renders them not only ineffectual, but displeasing, and even irritating.
entries.84d643209354136bc0442b2e36d0e13b26cc2bbd: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24235" type="x-p"/> But much increase is by the strength of the ox - The ox is the most profitable of all the beasts used in husbandry. Except merely for speed, he is almost in every respect superior to the horse. <div eID="gen24235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24236" type="x-p"/> 1. He is longer lived. <div eID="gen24236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24237" type="x-p"/> 2. Scarcely liable to any diseases. <div eID="gen24237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24238" type="x-p"/> 3. He is steady, and always pulls fair in his gears. <div eID="gen24238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24239" type="x-p"/> 4. He lives, fattens, and maintains his strength on what a horse will not eat, and therefore is supported on one third the cost. <div eID="gen24239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24240" type="x-p"/> 5. His manure is more profitable. <div eID="gen24240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24241" type="x-p"/> 6. When he is worn out in his labor his flesh is good for the nourishment of man, his horns of great utility, and his hide almost invaluable. <div eID="gen24241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24242" type="x-p"/> It might be added, he is little or no expense in shoeing, and his gears are much more simple, and much less expensive, than those of the horse. In all large farms oxen are greatly to be preferred to horses. Have but patience with this most patient animal, and you will soon find that there is much increase by the strength and labor of the ox.
entries.de542191595a31c35acdd03e9e7df5db999a9ad7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24243" type="x-p"/> A scorner seeketh wisdom - I believe the scorner means, in this book, the man that despises the counsel of God; the infidel. Such may seek wisdom; but he never can find it, because he does not seek it where it is to be found; neither in the teaching of God's Spirit, nor in the revelation of his will.
entries.1a78c1ba792f1d87450fd299414ed57872e5a1db: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24244" type="x-p"/> When thou perceivest not - the lips of knowledge - Instead of דעת daath, knowledge, several MSS. have שקר sheker, a lie. How this reading came I cannot conjecture. The meaning of the adage is plain: Never associate with a vain, empty fellow, when thou perceivest he can neither convey nor receive instruction.
entries.48c76a2fa7d10d5686a51a40f49cf1784c9998a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24245" type="x-p"/> Is to understand his way - Instead of הבין habin, to understand, הכין hachin, to Direct his way, is found in one MS. It makes a very good sense.
entries.4da34928ac7afde2c684399d8f2e48b98a39d464: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24246" type="x-p"/> Fools make a mock at sin - And only fools would do so. But he that makes a sport of sinning, will find it no sport to suffer the vengeance of an eternal fire. Some learned men by their criticisms have brought this verse into embarrassments, out of which they were not able to extricate it. I believe we shall not come much nearer the sense than our present version does.
entries.b4b9de292b5d9c9a885da62f599cb032e4dfedc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24247" type="x-p"/> The heart knoweth his own bitterness - מרת נפשו morrath naphsho, "The bitterness of its soul." Under spiritual sorrow, the heart feels, the soul feels; all the animal nature feels and suffers. But when the peace of God is spoken to the troubled soul, the joy is indescribable; the whole man partakes of it. And a stranger to these religious feelings, to the travail of the soul, and to the witness of the Spirit, does not intermeddle with them; he does not understand them: indeed they may be even foolishness to him, because they are spiritually discerned.
entries.5b9c0a2adf20f1717ca63197a1925ade33c187d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24248" type="x-p"/> There is a way which seemeth right unto a man - This may be his easily besetting sin, the sin of his constitution, the sin of his trade. Or it may be his own false views of religion: he may have an imperfect repentance, a false faith, a very false creed; and he may persuade himself that he is in the direct way to heaven. Many of the papists, when they were burning the saints of God in the flames at Smithfield, thought they were doing God service! And in the late Irish massacre, the more of the Protestants they piked to death, shot, or burnt, the more they believed they deserved of God's favor and their Church's gratitude. But cruelty and murder are the short road, the near way, to eternal perdition.
entries.ca52f8f2975da3c0c9927991856d6eadf20e7831: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24249" type="x-p"/> Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful - Many a time is a smile forced upon the face, when the heart is in deep distress. And it is a hard task to put on the face of mirth, when a man has a heavy heart.
entries.b46a6db126a36932434516dd6365049259f0a2a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24250" type="x-p"/> The backslider in heart shall be filled with his own ways - <div eID="gen24250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24251" type="x-p"/> 1. Who is the backslider? סוג sug. <div eID="gen24251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24252" type="x-p"/> 1. The man who once walked in the ways of religion, but has withdrawn from them. <div eID="gen24252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24253" type="x-p"/> 2. The man who once fought manfully against the world, the devil, and the flesh; but has retreated from the battle, or joined the enemy. <div eID="gen24253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24254" type="x-p"/> 3. The man who once belonged to the congregation of the saints, but is now removed from them, and is set down in the synagogue of Satan. <div eID="gen24254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24255" type="x-p"/> 2. But who is the backslider in Heart? <div eID="gen24255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24256" type="x-p"/> 1. Not he who was surprised and overcome by the power of temptation, and the weakness of his own heart. <div eID="gen24256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24257" type="x-p"/> 2. But he who drinks down iniquity with greediness. <div eID="gen24257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24258" type="x-p"/> 3. Who gives cheerful way to the bent of his own nature, and now delights in fulfilling the lusts of the flesh and of the mind. <div eID="gen24258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24259" type="x-p"/> 4. Who loves sin as before he loved godliness. <div eID="gen24259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24260" type="x-p"/> 3. What are his own ways? Folly, sin, disappointment, and death; with the apprehension of the wrath of God, and the sharp twingings of a guilty conscience. <div eID="gen24260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24261" type="x-p"/> 4. What is implied in being filled with his own ways? Having his soul saturated with folly, sin, and disappointment. At last ending here below in death, and then commencing an eternal existence where the fire is not quenched, and under the influence of that worm that never dieth. Alas, alas! who may abide when God doeth this? <div eID="gen24261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24262" type="x-p"/> And a good man shall be satisfied from himself - <div eID="gen24262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24263" type="x-p"/> 1. Who is the good man? (איש טוב ish tob). <div eID="gen24263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24264" type="x-p"/> 1. The man whose heart is right with God, whose tongue corresponds to his heart, and whose actions correspond to both. <div eID="gen24264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24265" type="x-p"/> 2. The man who is every thing that the sinner and backslider are not. <div eID="gen24265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24266" type="x-p"/> 2. He shall be satisfied from himself - he shall have the testimony of his own conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, he has his conversation among men. <div eID="gen24266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24267" type="x-p"/> 3. He shall have God's Spirit to testify with his spirit that he is a child of God. He hath the witness in himself that he is born from above. The Spirit of God in his conscience, and the testimony of God in his Bible, show him that he belongs to the heavenly family. It is not from creeds or confessions of faith that he derives his satisfaction: he gets it from heaven, and it is sealed upon his heart.
entries.cea8fcd551b12eec8c5c25a6cb7c0048929b5496: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24268" type="x-p"/> A wise man feareth - He can never trust in himself, though he be satisfied from himself. He knows that his suffiency is of God; and he has that fear that causes him to depart from evil, which is a guardian to the love he feels. Love renders him cautious; the other makes him confident. His caution leads him from sin; his confidence leads him to God.
entries.15244384c707d6d40cff1a274cf6131f9882d223: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24269" type="x-p"/> He that is soon angry - קצר אפים ketsar appayim, "short of nostrils:" because, when a man is angry, his nose is contracted, and drawn up towards his eyes. <div eID="gen24269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24270" type="x-p"/> Dealeth foolishly - He has no time for reflection; he is hurried on by his passions, speaks like a fool, and acts like a madman.
entries.54b1f3ce0aa279f83ea47d53fec6649d9c81c161: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24271" type="x-p"/> The evil bow before the good - They are almost constrained to show them respect; and the wicked, who have wasted their substance with riotous living, bow before the gates of the righteous - of benevolent men - begging a morsel of bread.
entries.b4ec1138b847fb377e6ebf2e57cb64d7cce71f97: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24272" type="x-p"/> But the rich hath many friends - Many who speak to him the language of friendship; but if they profess friendship because he is rich, there is not one real friend among them. There is a fine saying of Cicero on this subject: Ut hirundines festivo tempore praesto sunt, frigore pulsae recedunt: ita falsi amici sereno tempore praesto sunt: simul atque fortunae hiemem viderint, evolant omnes - Lib. iv., ad Herenn. "They are like swallows, who fly off during the winter, and quit our cold climates; and do not return till the warm season: but as soon as the winter sets in, they are all off again." So Horace: - <div eID="gen24272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24273" type="x-p"/> Donec eris felix, multos numerabis amicos:Nullus ad amissas ibit amicus opes. "As long as thou art prosperous, thou shalt have many friends: but who of them will regard thee when thou hast lost thy wealth?"
entries.796481e632dde1d04234994ec991ddc02ea62236: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24274" type="x-p"/> He that despiseth his neighbor sinneth - To despise a man because he has some natural blemish is unjust, cruel, and wicked. He is not the author of his own imperfections; they did not occur through his fault or folly; and if he could, he would not retain them. It is, therefore, unjust and wicked to despise him for what is not his fault, but his misfortune. <div eID="gen24274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24275" type="x-p"/> But he that hath mercy on the poor - Who reproaches no man for his poverty or scanty intellect, but divides his bread with the hungry - happy is he; the blessing of God, and of them that were ready to perish, shall come upon him.
entries.a0760978b50fbb5c983cf10664bbebe4a0eb51de: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24276" type="x-p"/> In all labor there is profit - If a man work at his trade, he gains by it; if he cultivate the earth, it will yield an increase; and in proportion as he labors, so will be his profit: but he who talks much labors little. And a man words is seldom a man of deeds. Less talk and more work, is one of our own ancient advices.
entries.8cafbecf49c84b3e958cb10f58227deb6e9f4e51: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24277" type="x-p"/> But the foolishness of fools is folly - The Targum reads, The honor of fools is folly. The fool, from his foolishness, produces acts of folly. This appears to be the meaning.
entries.15029552ab36b3e51d852cf962424d69b482e816: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24278" type="x-p"/> In the fear of the Lord is strong confidence - From this, and from genuine Christian experience, we find that the fear of God is highly consistent with the strongest confidence in his mercy and goodness.
entries.0415647cc030e126218915c8b58db71b059b6dfe: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24279" type="x-p"/> The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life - מקור חיים mekor chaiyim, the vein of lives. Another allusion to the great aorta which carries the blood from the heart to all the extremities of the body. Of this phrase, and the tree of lives, Solomon is particularly fond. See on <reference osisRef="Pro.4.23">Pro 4:23</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Pro.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference> (note).
entries.853cfe864ba223858315d5a47f64c6fb9d749ae1: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24280" type="x-p"/> In the multitude of people - It is the interest of every state to promote marriage by every means that is just and prudent; and to discourage, disgrace, and debase celibacy; to render bachelors incapable, after a given age, of all public employments: and to banish nunneries and monasteries from all parts of their dominions; - they have ever, from their invention, contributed more to vice than virtue; and are positively point blank against the law of God.
entries.4ecf338b094393095c1e241314ce35563741d3f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen24280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24281" type="x-p"/> That is hasty of spirit - קצר רוח ketsar ruach, "the short of spirit;" one that is easily irritated; and, being in a passion, he is agitated so as to be literally short of breath. Here put in opposition to ארך אפים erech appayim, long of nostrils; see on <reference osisRef="Pro.14.17">Pro 14:17</reference> (note); and of the same import with St. Paul's μακροθυμια, longsuffering, longmindedness. See on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2">Eph 4:2</reference> (note).
entries.4e0b711cbc8faf686dc2bd589c2a49af02db6301: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24282" type="x-p"/> A sound heart is the life of the flesh - A healthy state of the blood, and a proper circulation of that stream of life, is the grand cause, in the hand of God, of health and longevity. If the heart be diseased, life cannot be long continued.
entries.73b803b80662cb2606a52f56f2f8150f5414fa7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen24282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24283" type="x-p"/> He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker - Because the poor, or comparatively poor, are, in the order of God, a part of the inhabitants of the earth; and every man who loves God will show mercy to the poor, for with this God is peculiarly delighted. The poor have we ever with us, for the excitement and exercise of those benevolent, compassionate, and merciful feelings, without which men had been but little better than brutes.
entries.f61a20f043363b0a617937df9f0b6d059fd4ab12: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen24283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24284" type="x-p"/> The wicked is driven away in his wickedness - He does not leave life cheerfully. Poor soul! Thou hast no hope in the other world, and thou leavest the present with the utmost regret! Thou wilt not go off; but God will drive thee. <div eID="gen24284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24285" type="x-p"/> But the righteous hath hope in his death - He rejoiceth to depart and be with Christ: to him death is gain; he is not reluctant to go - he flies at the call of God.
entries.c3490b7f41365d7e2e76e1b3c4686f9797a461d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen24285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24286" type="x-p"/> But sin is a reproach to any people - I am satisfied this is not the sense of the original, וחסד לאמים חטאת vechesed leummim chattath; which would be better rendered, And mercy is a sin-offering for the people. The Vulgate has, Miseros autem facit populos peccatum, "sin makes the people wretched." Ελασσονουσι δε φυλας ἁμαρτιαι; "But sins lessen the tribes." - Septuagint. So also the Syriac and Arabic. The plain meaning of the original seems to be, A national disposition to mercy appears in the sight of God as a continual sin-offering. Not that it atones for the sin of the people; but, as a sin-offering is pleasing in the sight of the God of mercy, so is a merciful disposition in a nation. This view of the verse is consistent with the purest doctrines of free grace. And what is the true sense of the words, we should take at all hazards and consequences: we shall never trench upon a sound creed by a literal interpretation of God's words. No nation has more of this spirit than the British nation. It is true, we have too many sanguinary laws; but the spirit of the people is widely different. <div eID="gen24286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24287" type="x-p"/> If any one will contend for the common version, he has my consent; and I readily agree in the saying, Sin is the reproach of any people. It is the curse and scandal of man. Though I think what I have given is the true meaning of the text.
entries.36c4095991dd5aa6c43d290d15d5a9a45cbe1919: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen24287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24288" type="x-p"/> The king's favor is toward a wise servant - The king should have an intelligent man for his minister; a man of deep sense, sound judgment, and of a feeling, merciful disposition. He who has not the former will plunge the nation into difficulties; and he who has not the latter will embark her in disastrous wars. Most wars are occasioned by bad ministers, men of blood, who cannot be happy but in endeavoring to unchain the spirit of discord. Let every humane heart pray, Lord, scatter thou the people who delight in war! Amen - so be it. Selah!  <chapter eID="Prov.14"/> <div eID="gen24288" type="x-p"/>

entries.9c14659462eec6fb6b8eab31377b41381db0eb42: <reference osisRef="Prov.14.1">Pro 14:1</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.14.1">1</reference> The wisdom of the woman buildeth her house,    And folly teareth it down with its own hands. <div eID="gen11093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11094" type="x-p"/> Were it חכמות נשׁים, after Jdg 5:29, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">Isa 19:11</reference>, then the meaning would be: the wise among women, each of them buildeth her house. But why then not just אשּׁה חכמה, as <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.2">2Sa 14:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.35.25">Exo 35:25</reference>? The Syr., Targum, and Jerome write <hi type="italic">sapiens mulier</hi>. And if the whole class must be spoken of, why again immediately the individualizing in בּנתה? The lxx obliterates that by its ᾠκοδόμησαν. And does not אוּלת [folly] in the contrasted proverb (1b) lead us to conclude on a similar abstract in 1a? The translators conceal this, for they translate אולת personally. Thus also the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. and Luther; אוּלת is, says Kimchi, an adj. like עוּרת, <hi type="italic">caeca</hi>. But the linguistic usage does not point אויל with אוילי to any אוּל. It is true that a fem. of אויל does not occur; there is, however, also no place in which אולת may certainly present itself as such. Thus also חכמות must be an abstr.; we have shown at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pro 1:20</reference> how חכמות, as neut. plur., might have an abstr. meaning. But since it is not to be perceived why the poet should express himself so singularly, the punctuation חכמות is to be understood as proceeding from a false supposition, and is to be read חכמות, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Pro 9:1</reference> (especially since this passage rests on the one before us). Fleischer says: “to build the house is figuratively equivalent to, to regulate well the affairs of a house, and to keep them in a good condition; the contrary, to tear down the house, is the same contrast as the Arab. 'amârat âlbyt and kharab albyt. Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in Burckhardt’s <hi type="italic">Sprüchw</hi>. 217, harrt ṣabrt bythâ 'amârat, a good woman (<hi type="italic">ein braves Weib</hi>) has patience (with her husband), and thereby she builds up her house (at the same time an example of the use of the preterite in like general sentences for individualizing); also No. 430 of the same work: 'amârat âlbyt wla kharâbt, it is becoming to build the house, not to destroy it; cf. in the Thousand and One Nights, where a woman who had compelled her husband to separate from her says: âna âlty 'amalt hadhâ barwḥy wâkhrnt byty bnfsy. Burckhardt there makes the remark: 'amârat âlbyt denotes the family placed in good circumstances - father, mother, and children all living together happily and peacefully.” This conditional relation of the wife to the house expresses itself in her being named as house-wife (cf. <hi type="italic">Hausehre</hi> [= honour of a house] used by Luther, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.13">Psa 68:13</reference>), to which the Talmudic דּביתי (= <hi type="italic">uxor mea</hi>) answers; the wife is noted for this, and hence is called עיקר הבית, the root and foundation of the house; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Buxtorf’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>. col. 301. In truth, the oneness of the house is more dependent on the mother than on the father. A wise mother can, if her husband be dead or neglectful of his duty, always keep the house together; but if the house-wife has neither understanding nor good-will for her calling, then the best will of the house-father cannot hinder the dissolution of the house, prudence and patience only conceal and mitigate the process of dissolution - folly, viz., of the house-wife, always becomes more and more, according to the degree in which this is a caricature of her calling, the ruin of the house.
entries.ac2a30459e7ba423515735f218f4accbe2047ca5: <reference osisRef="Prov.14.2">Pro 14:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.14.2">2</reference> He walketh in his uprightness who feareth Jahve,    And perverse in his ways is he that despiseth Him. <div eID="gen11094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11095" type="x-p"/> That which syntactically lies nearest is also that which is intended; the ideas standing in the first place are the predicates. Wherein it shows itself, and whereby it is recognised, that a man fears God, or stands in a relation to Him of indifference instead of one of fear and reverence, shall be declared: the former walketh in his uprightness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, so far as the consciousness of duty which animates him prescribes; the latter in his conduct follows no higher rule than his own lust, which drives him sometimes hither and sometimes thither. הולך בּישׁרו .rehtih (cf. ישׁר הולך, Mic 2:7) is of kindred meaning with הולך בּתמּו, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.6">Pro 28:6</reference> (הולך בּתּום, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.9">Pro 10:9</reference>), and הולך נכחו, Isa 57:2. The connection of נלוז דּרכיו follows the scheme of 2Ki 18:37, and not <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.32">2Sa 15:32</reference>, Ewald, §288c. If the second word, which particularizes the idea of the first, has the reflexive suff. as here, then the accusative connection, or, as <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>, the prepositional, is more usual than the genitive. Regarding לוּז, <hi type="italic">flectere, inclinare</hi> (a word common to the author of chap. 1-9), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 2:15. With בּוזהוּ, cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1Sa 2:30</reference>; the suffix without doubt refers to God, for בוזהו is the word that stands in parallel contrast to 'ירא ה.
entries.3456716751213d22626969346dde18e7f227d7ae: <reference osisRef="Prov.14.3">Pro 14:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.14.3">3</reference> In the mouth of the fool is a switch of pride;    But the lips of the wise preserve them. <div eID="gen11095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11096" type="x-p"/> The noun חטר (Aram. חוּטרא, Arab. khiṭr), which besides here occurs only at <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference>, meaning properly a brandishing (from חטר = Arab. khatr, to brandish, to move up and down or hither and thither, whence âlkhṭtâr, the brandisher, poet. the spear), concretely, the young elastic twig, the switch, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the slender flexible shoot.
