They discredit and waste their little portion of wisdom (instead of thinking on its increase) by obtrusive ostentatious babbling.
entries.d4f13fdb275d4b4cec76de7501068d92036f4a66: <reference osisRef="Prov.14.34">Pro 14:34</reference> <div eID="gen11151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11152" type="x-p"/> Two proverbs follow regarding the state and its ruler: 34 Righteousness exalteth a nation,      And sin is a disgrace to the people. <div eID="gen11152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11153" type="x-p"/> The Hebr. language is richer in synonyms of “the people” than the German. גּוי (formed like the non-bibl. מוי, water, and נוי, corporealness, from גּוה, to extend itself from within outward; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.9.3">Pro 9:3</reference>, גּפּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">Pro 10:13</reference>, גּו) is, according to the <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>., like <hi type="italic">natio</hi> the people, as a mass swollen up from a common origin, and עם, 28a (from עמם, to bind), the people as a confederation held together by a common law; לאם (from לאם, to unite, bind together) is the mass (multitude) of the people, and is interchanged sometimes with גוי, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">Gen 25:23</reference>, and sometimes with עם, Pro 14:28. In this proverb, לאמּים stands indeed intentionally in the plur., but not גוי, with the plur. of which גּוים, the idea of the non-Israelitish nations, too easily connects itself. The proverb means all nations without distinction, even Israel (cf. under <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>) not excluded. History everywhere confirms the principle, that not the numerical, nor the warlike, nor the political, nor yet the intellectual and the so-called civilized greatness, is the true greatness of a nation, and determines the condition of its future as one of progress; but this is its true greatness, that in its private, public, and international life, צדקה, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, conduct directed by the will of God, according to the norm of moral rectitude, rules and prevails. Righteousness, good manners, and piety are the things which secure to a nation a place of honour, while, on the contrary, חטּאת, sin, viz., prevailing, and more favoured and fostered than contended against in the consciousness of the moral problem of the state, is a disgrace to the people, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it lowers them before God, and also before men who do not judge superficially or perversely, and also actually brings them down. רומם, to raise up, is to be understood after <reference osisRef="Isa.1.2">Isa 1:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.4">Pro 23:4</reference>, and is to be punctuated תּרומם, with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> of the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., and the העמדה-sign with the Tsere of the last syllable. Ben-Naphtali punctuates thus: תּרומם. In 34b all the artifices of interpretation (from Nachmani to Schultens) are to be rejected, which interpret חסד as the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. (ἔλεος δὲ λαῶν ἁμαρτία) in its predominant Hebrew signification. It has here, as at <reference osisRef="Lev.20.17">Lev 20:17</reference> (but not <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference>), the signification of the Syr. chesdho, <hi type="italic">opprobrium</hi>; the Targ. חסדּא, or more frequently חסּוּדא, as among Jewish interpreters, is recognised by Chanan'el and Rashbam. That this חסד is not foreign to the <hi type="italic">Mishle</hi> style, is seen from the fact that חסּד, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.10">Pro 25:10</reference>, is used in the sense of the Syr. chasedh. The synon. Syr. chasam, <hi type="italic">invidere, obtrectare</hi>, shows that these verbal stems are formed from the R. הס, <hi type="italic">stringere</hi>, to strike. Already it is in some measure perceived how חסד, Syr. chasadh, Arab. hasada, may acquire the meaning of violent love, and by the mediation of the jealousy which is connected with violent love, the signification of grudging, and thus of reproach and of envy; yet this is more manifest if one thinks of the root-signification stringere, in the meaning of loving, as referred to the subject, in the meanings of disgrace and envy, as from the subject directed to others. Ewald (§51c) compares חסל and חסר, Ethiop. chasra, in the sense of <hi type="italic">carpere</hi>, and on the other side חסה in the sense of “to join;” but חסה does not mean to join (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Psa 2:12</reference>) and instead of <hi type="italic">carpere</hi>, the idea more closely connected with the root is that of <hi type="italic">stringere</hi>, cf. <hi type="italic">stringere folia ex arboribus</hi> (Caesar), and <hi type="italic">stringere</hi> (to diminish, to squander, strip) <hi type="italic">rem ingluvie</hi> (Horace, <hi type="italic">Sat</hi>. i. 2. 8). The lxx has here read חסר (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.22">Pro 28:22</reference>), diminution, decay, instead of חסד (shame); the <hi type="italic">quid pro quo</hi> is not bad, the Syr. accepts it, and the <hi type="italic">miseros facit</hi> of Jerome, and Luther’s <hi type="italic">verderben</hi> (destruction) corresponds with this phrase better than with the common traditional reading which Symmachus rightly renders by ὄνειδος.
entries.6d2c60b30b159a7c21d74a0ad96d4a963a81bf43: <reference osisRef="Prov.14.35">Pro 14:35</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.14.35">35</reference> The king’s favour is towards a prudent servant,      And his wrath visits the base. <div eID="gen11153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11154" type="x-p"/> Regarding the contrasts משׂכּיל and מבישׁ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.5">Pro 10:5</reference>; cf. Pro 12:4. The substantival clause 35a may mean: the king’s favour has (possesses)..., as well as: it is imparted to, an intelligent servant; the arrangement of the words is more favourable to the latter rendering. In 35b the gender of the verb is determined by attraction after the pred., as is the case also at <reference osisRef="Gen.31.8">Gen 31:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.31">Job 15:31</reference>, Ewald, §317c. And “his wrath” is equivalent to is the object of it, cf. 22b, Pro 13:18. The syntactical character of the clause does not permit the supplying of ל from 35a. Luther’s translation proceeds only apparently from this erroneous supposition. <div eID="gen11154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11155" type="x-p"/> We take these verses together as forming a group which begins with a proverb regarding the good and evil which flows from the tongue, and closes with a proverb regarding the treasure in which blessing is found, and that in which no blessing is found.  <chapter eID="Prov.14"/> <div eID="gen11155" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 EVery wise woman <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He speaks of the <ns0:hi>Woman</ns0:hi> not to exclude the Man, of whom this is no less true, but because the Women, especially in those times, were very industrious in managing their Husbands Estates, of which see <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 31.</ns0:note> buildeth her house <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Maintaineth and improveth her Family and Estate, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 1. 21. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 11. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 127. 1.</ns0:note>, but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either by her idleness and not using her hands, or by her foolish and sinful courses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 He that walketh in his uprightness <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Whose conversation is sincerely pious and righteous. The design of this Proverb and Verse is to shew, that God doth, and men may judge of mens outward professions and inward dispositi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons by the common course of their lives.</ns0:note>, feareth the LORD <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 12. 4.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:hi>he that is</ns0:hi> perverse in his ways, despiseth him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Plainly declares that he doth not fear God, but despise him, and his commands, and threatnings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 In the mouth of the foolish <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a rod of pride <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">His proud and insolent speeches as they are like a Rod, offen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sive and injurious to others, so they make a Rod for their own Backs, by provoking God and men against them. Which sense seems most probable both from the opposite Clause, and by com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paring this place with <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10. 13. & 26. 3. For this Phrase, <ns0:hi>The Rod of Pride,</ns0:hi> it may be compared with other like Phrases, as <ns0:hi>the foot of Pride,</ns0:hi> Psal. 36. 11. <ns0:hi>The scourge of the Tongue,</ns0:hi> Job 5. 21. and <ns0:hi>the Rod of the Mouth,</ns0:hi> Isa. 11. 4.</ns0:note>, but the lips of the wise shall preserve them <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">From that Rod.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Where no Oxen <ns0:hi>are,</ns0:hi> the crib <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> clean <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Barn or Stable is empty of food for Cattel, and much more for Man, whose food is more scarce and dear.                      </ns0:note> A faithful witness will not lie <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To wit, in common discourse and conversation, whereby he sheweth his love to truth, and giveth assurance that when he is called to be a Witness, he will be true and faithful.</ns0:note>, but a false witness will utter lies <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, as the words lie in the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>And,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>But</ns0:hi> he that <ns0:hi>will utter lies</ns0:hi> (that accustometh himself to lying) is or will be <ns0:hi>a false Witness,</ns0:hi> when occasion requires it. Having debauched his Conscience by daily lying he is thereby prepared and disposed to false-witness-bearing. Compare <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 12. 17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 A scorner <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">A proud, self-conceited, and profane Person.</ns0:note> seeketh wisdom and <ns0:hi>findeth it</ns0:hi> not <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Because he doth not seek it aright, to wit, sincerely, and earnestly, and sea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonably, and in a constant and diligent use of all the means which God hath appointed to that end, and with an honest intention of employing his knowledge to the service of God, and the further<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance of his practice of Religion.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8. 9.</ns0:note> knowledge <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> easy unto him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Is plain and easily attained by him.</ns0:note> that understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That knoweth and is deeply sensible of his own want of knowledge, and of the great worth and necessity of knowledge, which will make him use all possible means to it, and, among other ways, pray earnestly to God for it. Or, that is honest and pious: for words of knowledge are oft understood practically, especially in this Book.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Go from the presence of a foolish man <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Avoid the company and conversation of ungodly men.</ns0:note>, when thou perceivest not <ns0:hi>in him</ns0:hi> the lips of knowledg <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">When they break forth into foolish or wicked discourses, left thou either be infected by them, or seem to approve of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 The wisdom of the prudent <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> to understand his way <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">It consists not in vain Speculations, nor in a curious prying into other mens matters, nor in cunning arts of deceiving others, but in a diligent study of his own duty, and of the way to true and eternal happiness.</ns0:note>, but the folly of fools <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> deceit <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The wit of ungodly men, which, though they account their Wisdom, is really their folly, is employed one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly in finding out ways of over-reaching and deceiving others, and themselves too.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 10. 23.</ns0:note> Fools <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Wicked men, as appears from their opposition to the <ns0:hi>righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous</ns0:hi> in the next Clause.</ns0:note> make a mock at sin <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Please and sport themselves with their own and other mens sins, which is an high offence and provocation to God and men. Or, as others render it, <ns0:hi>excuse</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>cover sin,</ns0:hi> sin against God or men, and then justifie or extenuate their sins, which is to double the injury. Possibly this Clause may be thus rendred, <ns0:hi>Sin deludes or makes a mock of Fools,</ns0:hi> or sinners, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poseth them to shame and contempt, which is fitly opposed to <ns0:hi>favour</ns0:hi> in the next Clause. And thus two Ancient and Learned In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpreters, <ns0:hi>Aquila</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Theodotion,</ns0:hi> render it. And this suits exactly with the Hebrew words, whereas in the other Translation the Noun and Verb governed by it are of divers Numbers, which though somtimes it be allowed, yet is not to be supposed without necessity. But this I submit to the learned and judicious.</ns0:note>, but among the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 21. 10.</ns0:note> righteous <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Who are so far from making a mock of sin, or excusing it, that they do not allow themselves to commit it.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> favour <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">They find favour both with God and men, as this very word thus generally expressed is used, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 11. 27. because they make conscience of ordering their lives so that they offend neither God nor men, or if they offend either, they heartily repent of it, so far are they from excus<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ng it or plea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing themselves with it. Or, there is <ns0:hi>good will,</ns0:hi> as the word pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perly and usually is taken: they have a real love, and are ready to do all Offices of kindness one to another, and therefore neither sin against others, nor rejoice in the sins of others.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 The heart knoweth <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>it<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terness of his Soul.</ns0:note> his own bitterness <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The sense of the Verse is this, The inward griefs and joys of mens Hearts, though somtimes they may be guessed at by out<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward signs, yet are not certainly known to any but a mans s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>lf. Compare 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2. 11. The scope of the Parable may be to keep men from murmuring under their own troubles or envying other mens happiness.</ns0:note>, and a stranger <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Any other Person without or beside a Mans self.</ns0:note> doth not intermeddle with his joy <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Doth not partake of it, nor understand it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 The house <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Their dwelling and family.</ns0:note> of the wicked shall be overthrown, but the tabernacle <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which is a weak, and poor, and unstable thing, soon reared up, and soon taken down, and is here opposed to the large, and strong, and magnificent House of wicked men.</ns0:note> of the upright shall prosper.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 16. 25.</ns0:note> There is a way which seemeth right unto a man <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">There are some evil actions or courses which men may think to be lawful and good, either through gross and affected igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rance; or through partiality or self-flattery; or through want of necessary diligence in examining them by the rule of God's will or word; all which are culpable causes of the mistake and therefore do not excuse the error.</ns0:note>, but the end thereof <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the ways of death <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The event sheweth that they were sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful and destructive.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5. 4.</ns0:note> the end of that mirth <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> heaviness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The outward signs of joy are commonly mixed with or end in real and hearty sorrow. The design of the Proverb is to declare the vanity of all worldly joys and comforts, and to teach men mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deration in them, and to persuade us to seek for more solid and durable joys.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 44. 18<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> The backslider in heart <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He who departeth from God and from the way of his Precepts with all his Heart, which implies the doing it upon deliberation, with free choice, and full purpose, and customary practice, as un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />godly men commonly do, and is opposed to the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>lips of humane frailty; for otherwise every sin is a revolt from God.</ns0:note> shall be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 31. & 12. 14.</ns0:note> filled with his own ways <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">With the fruit of his ways or doings, the punishment of his sins.</ns0:note>, and a good man <ns0:hi>shall be satisfied</ns0:hi> from himself <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From his ways, as appears by the opposition from the pious temper of his own Heart which cleaveth to the Lord, when the hearts of sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners forsake him, and from the holy and righteous course of his life, from which he shall receive unspeakable comfort and satis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />faction, both here and hereafter to all Eternity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 The simple <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either the harmless Man: or rather a foolish Man, because he is opposed to the prudent.</ns0:note> believeth every word <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Is easily deceived with the smooth words and fair pretences of false and deceitful men.</ns0:note>, but the prudent <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> looketh well to his going <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. to his own going, as this is generally understood, he or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dereth his conversation and dealings in the World with due circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spection, not considering so much what other men say as what he ought to do. Or, 2. to the going of the deceiver, whose the word in the former clause is suppos'd to be. So the sense is, he judgeth of mens words and professions by their conversations; which is a good rule.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:528" />16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch 22. 3.</ns0:note> A wise <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> feareth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Trembleth at God's judgments when they are either inflicted or threatned.</ns0:note>, and departeth from evil <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">From sin, which is the procuring cause of all cala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mities.</ns0:note>, but the fool rageth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Fretteth against God, or is enraged against his Messen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers who bring the threatning, or disquieteth himself in vain. Or <ns0:hi>transgresseth,</ns0:hi> as this Verb in its simple form and first conjugation commonly signifies, or, <ns0:hi>goeth on in sin constantly and resolutely,</ns0:hi> according to the <ns0:hi>Emphasis</ns0:hi> which this conjugation commonly adds to the simple Verb. And this is most fitly opposed to <ns0:hi>departing from evil,</ns0:hi> as being <ns0:hi>confident</ns0:hi> is opposed to <ns0:hi>fearing.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> and is confident <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Secure and insensible of his danger till God's judgments overtake him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:hi>He that is</ns0:hi> soon angry dealeth foolishly <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">His passion hurries him into many rash and foolish speeches and actions.</ns0:note>, and a man of wicked devices <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">One who suppresseth his passion, but designeth and meditateth revenge, watching for the fittest methods and op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portunities of executing it.</ns0:note> is hated <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Both by God and men, as being most deeply malicious and like the Devil, and most dangerous and pernicious to humane Society, whereas men that are soon angry give a Man warning and are quickly pacified, and therefore pitied and pardoned.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 The simple inherit folly <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">They possess it as their Inheritance or portion, holding it fast, improving it, delighting and glorying in it. In like manner <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> took God's <ns0:hi>Testimonies</ns0:hi> for his <ns0:hi>Heritage,</ns0:hi> Psal. 119. 111. where the word is the same: Withal he may imply that folly is Natural and Hereditary to them.</ns0:note>, but the prudent are crowned with knowledg <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">They place their honour and happiness in a sound and practical, and saving knowledge of God and of their own duty, and therefore earnestly pursue after it, and Heartily embrace it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 The evil bow before the good <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Giving honour to them, and supplicating their favour and help, either for supply of their wants, as being brought low for their sins, or for counsel or comfort, or for their prayers to God for them.</ns0:note>, and the wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed at the gates <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">As Clients, and Petitioners, and Beggers use to wait at the Doors, and Houses of Great and Potent men. The sense is, Good men shall have the preeminency over the wicked, oft-times in this life, when God sees it expedient, but assuredly in the next life.</ns0:note> of the righteous.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 19. 7.</ns0:note> The poor is hated <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Despised and abandoned, as hateful Persons and Things are.</ns0:note> even of his own neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Strictly so called, who is nearest to him, either by habi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation or by relation, and therefore most obliged to love and help him.</ns0:note>, but <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>many</ns0:hi> are <ns0:hi>the lovers of the Rich.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the rich <ns0:hi>hath</ns0:hi> many friends.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 He that despiset his neighbour <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That doth not pity and relieve the poor, as this is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plained in the next Clause, the word <ns0:hi>Neighbour</ns0:hi> being here general<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly taken for any Man, as it is most commonly used in Scripture; which not relieving him, proceeds from a contempt of his Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son.</ns0:note>, sinneth <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And therefore shall be punished for his inhumanity, which is opposed to his being <ns0:hi>happy</ns0:hi> in the next Clause.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 112. 9.</ns0:note> but he that hath mercy <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That sheweth his compassion by his bounty and relief.</ns0:note> on the poor, happy <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He doth a worthy action, and shall be blessed in his deed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 Do they not err <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">They do certainly err from the right way, and mistake their mark, and shall miss of that advantage and felicity which they pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise to themselves by such practices.</ns0:note> that devised <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That do not onely commit it but make it their design, and study, and business, that are Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tists or Masters in it, as the word signifies.</ns0:note> evil <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either 1. mischief to men. Or 2. any kind of wickedness against God or men; for the expression is general; and this seems best to agree to the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing Clause.</ns0:note>? but mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy and truth <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either 1. from men; Men shall deal truly and kindly with them, partly because such men by their carriage oblige them to do so, and partly because God inclineth their hearts to it. Or 2. from God to whom these two properties are jointly ascribed in divers places of Scripture.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>shall be to</ns0:hi> them that devise good <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">That designedly and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dustriously apply themselves to the doing of all good offices to God and men.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 In all labour there is profit, but the talk of the lips <ns0:hi>tendeth</ns0:hi> onely to penury <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Diligem labour is the ready way to riches, but idle talking, wherein too many spend most of their pretious time, will bring a Man to poverty.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 The crown of the wise <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> their riches <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">They are a singular advantage and ornament to them, partly as they make their Wisdom more regarded, when <ns0:hi>the poor Man's wisdom is despised,</ns0:hi> Eccles. 9. 16. and partly as they give a Man great opportunity to discover and exercise his Wisdom or Vertue by laying out his Riches to the honour and service of God, and to the great and manifold good of the World; which also highly tends to his own glory and happiness.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:hi>: but</ns0:hi> the foolishness of fools <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> folly <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">But as for rich fools, for to them the general word is to be restrained from the opposite Clause, their folly is not cured, but made worse and more mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fest by their riches. Their Riches find them Fools, and leave them Fools; they are not a Crown, but a reproach to them, and an occasion of their greater contempt. For the Phrase, we have the like in the Hebrew Text, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. 24. <ns0:hi>The Child</ns0:hi> Samuel was <ns0:hi>a Child.</ns0:hi> It is an elegant Figure called <ns0:hi>Antanaclasis</ns0:hi> used in all Au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thors.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Vers. 5.</ns0:note> A true witness delivereth Souls <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e</ns0:hi> Persons, to wit, such as are innocent from the mischief of false Accusations, by declaring the truth, which is sufficient for their Vindication.</ns0:note>, but a deceit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful <ns0:hi>witness</ns0:hi> speaketh lies <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To the injury and destruction of the Inno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cent, which is easily understood out of the former Clause, and from the practice of false Witnesses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26. In the fear of the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> strong confidence <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">A sure ground of confidence, or a strong refuge, as the next Clause explains it.</ns0:note>; and his children <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either 1. God's Children. Or 2. the Children of them that fear God, who are sufficiently understood out of the former Clause.</ns0:note> shall have a place of refuge.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 13. 12.</ns0:note> The fear of the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To preserve men from deadly and destructive courses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. In the multitude of people <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the kings honour <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Because it is an evidence of his wise and good government. Un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der <ns0:hi>honour</ns0:hi> he here comprehends also strength and safety, (as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears from the opposite Clause,) which depend much upon a Princes reputation. And <ns0:hi>honour</ns0:hi> may be here put for strength, as <ns0:hi>strength</ns0:hi> is put for honour or glory, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 8. 2. & 29. 1. & 96. 7.</ns0:note>, but in the want of people <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the destruction of the prince.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 <ns0:hi>He that is</ns0:hi> slow to wrath is of great understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Sheweth great and true wisdom in conquering his sinful and shameful passions.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but <ns0:hi>he</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> short of Spirit.</ns0:note> hasty of spirit, exalteth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>lifteth up,</ns0:hi> like a Banner, makes it known and visible to all men.</ns0:note> folly.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 A sound heart <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Free from envy and such like inordinate passions, which are commonly called <ns0:hi>the Diseases of the Soul,</ns0:hi> not onely in Sacred, but even in Heathen Writers, Or, as others render it, <ns0:hi>An healing Heart,</ns0:hi> mild, and merciful, and kind to others, which is opposed to envy.</ns0:note> is the lise of the flesh <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Procureth and maintaineth the health and vigor of the whole Body.</ns0:note>; but envy the rottenness of the bones <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It wasteth the Spirits, and consumeth even the strongest and most inward parts of the Body.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 17. 5. Mat. 25. 40, 45.</ns0:note> He that oppresseth the poor <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">That useth him hardly, as the Syriack renders it, that with-hold<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth from him that which is his due, either by the rules of strict justice or by the great Law of Charity, of which see <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3. 27. and so it is opposed to <ns0:hi>having Mercy</ns0:hi> in the next Clause.</ns0:note>, reproacheth his maker <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Whose Image the poor Man bears, which might challenge respect; <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 15. by whose counsel and providence he is made poor; 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 7. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 22. 2. and who hath declared himself to be their protector and avenger.</ns0:note>: but he that honoureth him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">His Image, and Works, and Laws.</ns0:note>, hath mercy on the poor <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Doth not onely forbear, oppressing or injuring of him, but affords him his pity and help.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 The wicked is driven away <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To wit, in his Death, as is gathered from the opposite Clause: <ns0:hi>driven away</ns0:hi> from God's favour and presence, and from the Society of the Just, and from all his hopes of Happiness both in this life and in the next. This expression notes that this is done suddenly, violently, and irresistibly, as the smoke or chaff are driven away by a strong Wind.</ns0:note> in his wickedness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>for his wickedness,</ns0:hi> Heb. <ns0:hi>in his evil,</ns0:hi> which may be understood of the evil of punishment; in the day of his cala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mity, when he shall flee to God for help.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 13. 15. & 19. 26. Ps. 23. 4. 1 Cor. 15. 19. 2 Cor. 1. 9.</ns0:note> but the righteous hath hope <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Of deliverance from it, or of great and everlasting advantage by it.</ns0:note> in his death <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">In his greatest dangers and distresses, yea even in I eath it self, which there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore he can receive with comfort and confidence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the heart, which is expressed by this very word, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 64. 6. and elsewhere. That Folly which is there instead of Wisdom: or, that small de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gree of Wisdom or Knowledg which they have.</ns0:note> of fools is made known <ns0:hi>n.</ns0:hi>

                        <ns0:hi>r</ns0:hi> They will pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lish it in all times and companies, without any consideration or dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cretion.</ns0:note>

                  <ns0:p n="34">34 Righteousness exalteth a nation <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Maketh it honourable in the Eyes of God, and of all other Nations, as it did the ancient Romans.</ns0:note>, but sin <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a reproach <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> to any people <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Brings contempt and ruine upon them by provoking both God and men against them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 The kings favour <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> toward a wise servant, but his wrath is <ns0:hi>against</ns0:hi> him <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap>. 17. 2.</ns0:note> that causeth shame <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Both to himself, by his foolish management of the Kings af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fairs commited to him, and to the King who made so foolish a choice of a Servant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
